title: Ox forgotten
hook: seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man alone at ease

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sixth picture: the herdsman riding home on the ox, playing the flute. Your line: riding home. What did you do lightly, just for the tune of it? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

The seventh picture has something missing. The herdsman is home now, sitting outside a small thatched hut. The sun is up. He looks rested, maybe half dozing. The whip and the rope lie idle, or hang on the wall. And the ox, the animal this whole series has been about, the one he searched for, tracked, glimpsed, caught, tamed and rode, is nowhere in the picture. He hasn't lost it. He's forgotten it. Today: ox forgotten.
screen: `HOME, OUTSIDE A THATCHED HUT.` → `WHIP AND ROPE LIE IDLE.` → `NO OX IN THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the ox was a way of speaking. The preface for this picture, in paraphrase, says the teaching is one, and the ox was only a temporary subject, something to point with. Like the moon coming out from behind the clouds, the preface says, what was there all along is simply clear now. The ox was never a separate creature out in the hills. It was a picture for something the herdsman had all along. Second, a raft is for crossing. In an early sutta, the Buddha uses a picture like this. A man builds a raft to cross a river. Once across, he doesn't hoist the raft onto his head and carry it on, however useful it was. He leaves it at the shore. Teachings help you cross, the Buddha said; they aren't for clinging to. The seventh picture puts the raft down. Third, forgetting is not losing. The man in the picture didn't misplace something precious. When a skill becomes yours, you stop thinking about it. A practiced cook doesn't recite the recipe. A good friend doesn't keep a ledger. The ox is forgotten because there's nothing left to manage. Fourth, there's still a man. The picture's full title, in Chinese, says the ox is forgotten and the person remains. He's still there, at ease, someone who has finished a long job. That detail matters for tomorrow, when even he will drop out of the frame. For today, the picture is restful: a quiet yard, a morning sun, tools hung up, and nothing more to chase.
screen: `THE OX WAS A WAY OF SPEAKING.` · `A RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · `FORGETTING IS NOT LOSING.` · `THE OX GONE, THE MAN REMAINS.` · then, large: `THE OX FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit down the way someone sits after finishing a long job. No technique today. Don't count the breath, don't watch for wandering, don't try to be calm. Set the rope down. If you catch yourself checking whether you're doing it right, notice that, and set that down too. Just rest, the way the herdsman rests in the sun outside his hut. Rest without effort. The bell holds the time.
Ox forgotten. The seventh oxherding picture: home and at ease, the herdsman no longer needs the ox, which was a way of pointing all along; the man remains. Today's word.
Your line: the ox forgotten. Today, find one thing you do well without thinking about it, and let it be easy, with no checking. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Zen teachers pair the seventh oxherding picture with the Buddha's parable of the raft to warn students against clinging even to their methods and to describe practice that no longer needs managing.

pairs: a temporary subject, a way of pointing

myth: in the seventh picture the herdsman has lost his ox
he hasn't lost it; there's simply nothing left to manage, so it's forgotten.
the preface calls the ox a temporary subject
the ox was a way of pointing at something the herdsman had all along.
the seventh picture shows no person at all
the ox is gone but the man remains; he drops out in the next picture.

fork.setup: you've crossed the river on a raft you built yourself. it served you well. what does the Buddha's parable say to do with it?
options: carry it on your head, in gratitude.
leave it at the shore and go on.
burn it so no one else uses it.
fork.reveal: in the parable the raft is left at the shore: teachings are for crossing over, not for clinging to. the seventh picture puts the ox down the same way.

original.note: Chinese (wangniu cunren): 'the ox forgotten, the person remains', the name of the seventh oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgetting the ox means the training failed.
what it means: the ox was a way of pointing; at home and at ease, there's nothing left to manage.
what a scholar hears: the full title says the ox is forgotten and the person remains, setting up the eighth picture, where both drop away.

notes: All quotations paraphrased. Check picture 7 preface: the dharma is one, the ox a temporary subject; the moon emerging from clouds image. Verse: home, the ox can rest, sun high, whip and rope idle in the thatched hut.
Raft parable (MN 22) paraphrased; voice calls it 'an early sutta, as later Buddhists remember it' to avoid a dating claim. Confirm framing.
Original 忘牛存人; pronunciation approximates Mandarin wangniu cunren.
